codes.name: Local pride
codes.definition: Use for expressions of civic pride: affection for local history, hospitality, traditions, sports, downtowns, distinctive places, family roots, “coming home,” and the feeling that the community has shared values or is recognized positively by outsiders.

children.name: Neighborly hospitality, generosity, and shared civic values
children.definition: Expressions of pride in a community’s character: residents see their town as welcoming, kind, inclusive, service-minded, mutually supportive, and guided by shared local or civic values.

I'd be proud, proud of this community for all the help and assistance and how people came together to help out a federal workforce during government shutdowns. That's one of the biggest reasons I'm proud to be living in Yankton these days.

evidence.text: So I grew up here, but I left for 35 years and spent 18 years in Bricktown in Oklahoma City operating the Bricktown Brewery. And on the day of the horrific thing at the Mirror Building, I was at work staff, everybody reacted. I saw the outpouring of how a community was just like, oh my gosh. Saw lines of people trying to donate water. Saw just so many incredible things. The most powerful was the Bricktown Brewery. At the time was probably the premier venue destination in Oklahoma City. It was very different than what it is right now. It's a lot more successful since I sold it. Okay. But at the time in 1995, we were kind of the centerpiece of Oklahoma City and downtown and somewhat a reflection of what was happening in Oklahoma City with maps and that. Look at a look at this venue. So many just horrible, horrible images. Terrible things that happened with the aftermath of the bombing. But also saw a community come together. And we had the honor of hosting every group of first responders that came from all over the country. Their last night before they flew out the next morning, there was a group of legislators that raised money. And then we also donated a lot. And we sealed off the upstairs that could hold as many as 1,000 people. And they just had their time to hug, cry, have a beer, have a bite to eat before they left. That in itself was powerful. The very last group that we entertained, I shouldn't say that the very last group that we hosted was the Oklahoma City fire and rescue. It was on a Saturday night. Our downstairs was packed. We were on a long way noisy. We were just a. Just a kind of a loud place. As these people came in and started walking upstairs, the whole place grew silent. At that time, as the first responders from Oklahoma City were walking upstairs, everybody stopped what they were doing. They stood up and they just applauded. And I'm telling you, there wasn't a dry tear in the house downstairs, but then as well as upstairs, because to see and just feel, I didn't go through any of that. Okay. Our role was to be in a support role. But to hear conversations that I overheard that night, they all went in the very back part of the bricktown brewery upstairs in what's called the red brick room. The building was built in 1909, and there's this huge wooden column. And on that wooden column, all the first responders before they left would do graffiti on it in a very obviously touching way. And Oklahoma City were the last ones to sign that. And to this day, I've begged them Plexiglas around that showcase. It put a title up to say what this is, because now if you just walk in there to eat or go to a function, you don't realize the history from that. So I believe that a lot of the reasons why I'm in Chickasha right now is because my role is to take what I saw and learned in a community investing in themselves, and then turn around and see what we can do here in Chickasha to implement that same type of attitude of investing in ourselves. And it's not through a map sales tax like Oklahoma City has, But it's through getting community to believe in ourselves that we can do things, and we are doing things, but do it in a way, when we look in the mirror, we're proud of our community, Very much like what Oklahoma City is experiencing.

children.definition:
Use when people discuss the coordination, logistics, funding, staffing, volunteer labor, collaboration, barriers, burnout, duplication, or long-term infrastructure needed to keep nonprofits, churches, pantries, housing supports, hospitals, family supports, and other local care systems functioning for people facing poverty, homelessness, illness, or household instability.

Community members who do volunteer work face burnout, time pressure, and added responsibility, including the burden of filling gaps in local government or public services.

Volunteer contributions that are essential to community functioning but go unnoticed, undercounted, or are not recognized as formal volunteering.

People may be willing to help but lack straightforward, welcoming, or feasible pathways into volunteer roles that match their abilities and circumstances.

Volunteering becomes difficult when what organizations need, what volunteers expect, and what the work actually requires do not line up.

Use when speakers express concern, frustration, or disappointment that too few residents show up for local civic life, voting, meetings, events, or volunteer work; that the same small group carries most community efforts; or that the shared expectation of volunteering and civic participation has weakened over time.

Volunteering is sustained by local pride, rural mutual aid norms, and community-rooted leaders who organize and model participation.

evidence.text: I think leadership needs to make sure that the doors are open and they almost need to go way out of their way to make sure doors are open. And when they do that and they allow, if you will, new people to have a seat at the table, then they need to listen to them. Don't just bring them there as a token representation, whether it be females or minorities or people with different lifestyles. Doesn't mean you agree with them. But I think you have to listen to them. And I think that's the role of leadership is to grow a community that can be rich in diversity, yet one in faith of what you're trying to accomplish. And then you do need to listen to them. Because even though I may say I understand exactly how tax increment financing works, this is going to be a great tool. We might have a farmer and a rancher out here that he doesn't really understand it and he just feels like it's being forced upon them. And sometimes they don't even want to listen. Even if you're like, I've got factual information. Your feelings are feelings, but it's their feelings. And so it's so difficult to have to build that consensus of we want to hear what everybody has to say, but we got to be trying to, we've got to be trying every single week, every month. And then as we see progress in our community, we also need to be reaching out and grabbing people. One of the things that leadership, Chickasha, Johnny's the co chair of that, that they do, that's just absolutely awesome is they take this class of 25 people every year and they bring them into Rotary and then instead of it just being a pitch for Rotary, they invite all the civic clubs in Chickasha and everybody gets five minutes, hey, this is what we do at the Lions Club. This is Altrusa. This is. And so those 25 people that have expressed interest in knowing more about Chickasha and being in a leadership row, they can hear about these different civic organizations and hopefully And I think our results show that most of them will find one and then get involved. But leadership has to open the doors and sometimes we've got to push people in there because that's how much their opinions count. In rural Oklahoma, too often it's the good old boys club. And I like to use the phrase stale, male and pale. And those are your decision makers in a lot of rural Oklahoma. So whether it's through the chamber or economic development, you have to have a conscience plan to include people that aren't in that stale, male and pale category, even though they may be part of your leaders. You've got to have a plan of how do we get others at the table and make sure they feel comfortable. And then we've got to have their input. It's not enough for them just to be sitting here. We may have to go extract that information out of them because we've all said it is. You know, we're going to look up here in 20 years and there's probably three of us here that probably won't be playing a significant role in Chickasha 20 years from now. Don't count on it.

It's the same things that we're talking about today. We're doubling our water treatment plant, we're doubling our waste treatment plan. You know, we're planning for the future. And I think. I think that's what's really important in the community is when the current leaders are planning for the next generation of residents. And that's how you continue to be a community that exists well and you progress and you provide for the future. And so, like I said, I'm kind of proud of our community because we don't see a lot of resistance towards. We do from time to time, but we don't see a lot of resistance to change.
